cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards
points: Linked to rewards, punishments, and remediation
distractors: Rankings of employees from best to worst, such as top 20% superior and bottom 10% needs improvement.
Behaviors employees must show, such as arriving on time and helping coworkers without being asked.
Goals employees set for themselves, such as learning a new skill or earning a certificate this year.

cards.front: What are the benefits of setting specific, challenging goals?
cards.answer: They focus attention, increase effort, sustain persistence through setbacks, and prompt new strategies.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.7 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards
points: Goals affect direction, effort, and persistence
Works for individuals, groups, units, and organizations
distractors: They lower stress, reduce effort needed, and let people avoid setbacks by choosing easy strategies.
They work only when tied to pay, since effort and persistence rise only with bonuses attached.
They replace the need for feedback, since a challenging goal tells people all they need to know.

cards.front: Which kind of goals produce the highest performance?
cards.answer: Specific and difficult goals, when the person is committed to them.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.7 · Motivational Concepts
cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards
points: 40+ years of goal-setting research
distractors: Vague 'do your best' goals, since they reduce pressure on people.
Easy goals, since early success builds momentum and confidence.
Specific and difficult goals, even when the person isn't committed.

cards.front: When is goal commitment highest?
cards.answer: When the person believes the goal is important and attainable.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.7 · Motivational Concepts
cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards
points: Commitment matters most for specific, difficult goals
Involve people in setting goals to build it
distractors: When the goal is set by the manager alone and kept secret.
When the goal is easy enough that no effort is required.
When the goal is tied to a bonus and is very difficult.

cards.front: What is self-efficacy, and how does it affect goal setting?
cards.answer: Belief in your own ability; it raises performance, the goals people set, and resilience after failure.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.7 · Motivational Concepts
cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards
points: Also shapes commitment and strategy choice
distractors: Belief in your team's ability; it lowers the goals people set but raises effort after small successes.
Your actual skill level; it sets the ceiling on performance regardless of what goals you set.
Confidence in your manager; it raises goal commitment but has no effect on resilience or effort.

cards.front: Why does goal setting work best with feedback?
cards.answer: Progress feedback shows whether effort is on track, so people can adjust strategy.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.7 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards; 8.4 Why Is Performance Management Important?
points: Goals without feedback are ineffective
distractors: Feedback replaces the goal, so people no longer need targets once they know their progress.
Feedback makes goals easier, so people lower their targets to keep feedback positive.
Feedback raises pay, so people work harder only when goals and feedback come with bonuses.

cards.front: How can goals backfire?
cards.answer: Overly ambitious or narrow goals can push unethical or risky behavior and crowd out safety and cooperation.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.7 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards
points: Mortgage volume goals and the 2008 crisis; Enron; Bausch & Lomb
Big goal-linked rewards may dampen intrinsic motivation
distractors: Easy goals backfire most, since they lead people to take risks and cut corners just to stay busy.
Goals backfire only when they're set by employees themselves rather than by managers above them.
Goals never backfire if they're SMART, since specific targets rule out unethical or risky behavior.

cards.front: How many priorities does Ritz-Carlton allow per unit, and why?
cards.answer: At most three, because beyond three you diffuse resources.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.7 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards
points: Balance financial and nonfinancial goals
distractors: At most five, so every department has its own priority.
At most one, because a single goal keeps people focused.
As many as needed, since more priorities raise effort.

cards.front: What did Cargill's Everyday Performance Management change?
cards.answer: It dropped the annual review for continuous recognition, team-owned performance talks, and coaching.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.7 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards
points: More useful feedback, less paperwork
distractors: It added a forced ranking system with annual ratings tied directly to each person's pay and bonus.
It replaced coaching with quarterly written reviews completed by HR staff rather than by managers.
It kept the annual review but made it self-rated, so employees scored their own work for the year.

cards.front: What is multisource (360-degree) assessment?
cards.answer: Gathering performance ratings from several sources: self, supervisor, peers, subordinates, and customers.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources
points: Supervisor ratings drive promotion decisions; others are mostly for development
distractors: Ranking employees from best to worst by comparing each person with every other person in the unit.
Rating employees on behaviorally anchored scales developed from critical incidents by job experts.
Gathering ratings only from the supervisor, who reviews the employee's work four times a year.

cards.front: What are the main sources of performance information?
cards.answer: Supervisor, self, peers or coworkers, subordinates (upward), and internal or external customers.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources
points: Choose and weight by credibility and opportunity to observe
distractors: Supervisor, HR, the CEO, the board of directors, and outside consultants hired by the company.
Self and supervisor only, since peers and subordinates aren't allowed to rate under federal law.
Customers alone, since they're the only source independent of internal politics and bias.

cards.front: What is task acquaintance?
cards.answer: The amount and type of work contact a rater has with the person being rated.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources
points: Raters can only judge what they've observed
The key test for choosing a source
distractors: How long a rater has worked at the company before rating anyone else.
How familiar a rater is with the rating form and the scales it uses.
How well a rater knows the employee socially, outside of work hours.

cards.front: What is the supervisor's role as a rating source?
cards.answer: The most common, expected source; rates performance, development needs, and promotion potential.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources
points: 'Challenge sessions' let supervisors scrutinize each other's ratings
distractors: The least common source, used only when peers and customers aren't available to rate.
A source that rates only interpersonal behavior, since bosses rarely see task performance.
An optional source that rates promotion potential but never development needs.

cards.front: What are the benefits and limits of self-assessment?
cards.answer: It opens dialogue and adds unseen information, but people misjudge themselves, too high or too low.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources
points: Often opens the appraisal meeting
distractors: It's highly accurate and replaces the supervisor's rating, since people know their own work best.
It's useful only for pay decisions, since people rate themselves honestly when money is at stake.
It's legally required for every review, but people consistently rate themselves lower than others.

cards.front: Why are peers valuable rating sources?
cards.answer: They see task and interpersonal behavior the boss misses, especially in interdependent work.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources
points: More honest when ratings are for development
Drop the highest and lowest peer ratings
distractors: They see only task results, so their ratings are most useful for setting pay and bonuses.
They rate more leniently than bosses, so their ratings improve morale across the team.
They know company strategy better than the boss, so they can judge goal alignment best.

cards.front: What are upward reviews, and what do they require?
cards.answer: Subordinates rating a manager's leadership and interpersonal behavior; anonymity is critical.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources
points: Fear of retaliation is the main limit
Many unanswered items can signal a problem
distractors: Managers rating their own bosses on strategy and results; it requires names on every rating.
Customers rating a manager's interpersonal behavior; it requires a written complaint process.
Subordinates rating each other's teamwork and output; it requires approval from HR first.

cards.front: What should external customers be asked to rate?
cards.answer: Interpersonal behavior, because they can't separate the employee from company rules and resources.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources
points: Customers broaden whom employees aim to please
distractors: Task results and productivity, since customers see output more clearly than anyone else.
The company's prices and policies, since customers know the rules better than employees.
Overall job performance, since customers can fully separate employees from company rules.

cards.front: Which cultures suit 360-degree feedback best?
cards.answer: Egalitarian cultures; it fits less well in hierarchical or paternalistic cultures.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources
points: Ratings must be accepted and seen as fair
distractors: Hierarchical cultures; it fits less well in egalitarian or individualistic cultures.
Paternalistic cultures; it fits less well where power is shared or flat in structure.
All cultures equally; it works the same wherever it's used, regardless of hierarchy.

cards.front: What is the difference between rating and ranking methods?
cards.answer: Rating compares each person to standards; ranking compares people to each other.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.9 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.9 Performance Measurement Methods; 8.11 Performance Ranking Methods
points: Rating: everyone can score high if deserved
Ranking: someone must be low even if all are excellent
distractors: Ranking compares each person to standards; rating compares people to each other.
Rating is used for pay; ranking is used only for training and development plans.
Rating uses numbers; ranking uses written essays and critical incident examples.

cards.front: What are essay appraisals and critical incidents?
cards.answer: Essay: a written description of strengths and weaknesses. Critical incidents: specific good and bad examples.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.9 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.9 Performance Measurement Methods
points: Both specific but hard to compare; incidents are time-consuming to record
distractors: Essay: specific good and bad examples. Critical incidents: a written description of strengths and weaknesses.
Essay: ratings on a scale from unsatisfactory to outstanding. Critical incidents: ranking best to worst.
Essay: picking statements with secret weights. Critical incidents: comparing each person with every other.

cards.front: What is a graphic rating scale?
cards.answer: Rating dimensions like quality or cooperation on a scale such as unsatisfactory to outstanding.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.9 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.9 Performance Measurement Methods
points: More reliable and comparable than essays
Best combined with essays and critical incidents
distractors: Scales where each point is anchored by a behavioral example from critical incidents.
Picking the best-fitting statement from a set with secret weights for each statement.
Ordering employees from best to worst, compared against each other on overall results.

cards.front: What are behaviorally anchored rating scales (BARS)?
cards.answer: Scales where each point is anchored by a behavioral example, developed from critical incidents.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.9 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.9 Performance Measurement Methods
points: Example: 5 = anticipates needs; 1 = does only what's told
distractors: Scales rating how often each desired behavior occurs, giving more feedback than graphic ones.
Rating dimensions like quality on a scale from unsatisfactory to outstanding, with no examples.
Picking the best-fitting statement from a set with secret weights to reduce rater bias.

cards.front: What are behavioral observation scales (BOS)?
cards.answer: Scales rating how often each desired behavior occurs, giving more feedback than BARS.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.9 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.9 Performance Measurement Methods
points: Example: 5 = 95-100% of the time
distractors: Scales where each point is anchored by a behavioral example from critical incidents.
Rating dimensions on a scale from unsatisfactory to outstanding, with no examples.
Ranking employees by how often they show each behavior compared to their peers.

cards.front: What is forced-choice rating?
cards.answer: Picking the best-fitting statement from a set with secret weights; reduces bias but can't be shared as feedback.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.10 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.10 Performance Rating Methods: Forced Choice, Checklist, Standards, and Objectives
points: Raters may feel distrusted; can be faked
distractors: Fitting ratings to a set curve, like 20/70/10; it reduces leniency but erodes teamwork among good performers.
Rating how often each desired behavior occurs; it gives specific feedback but takes a long time to develop.
Comparing each person with every other person; it's thorough but becomes unwieldy in very large groups.

cards.front: What is management by objectives (MBO)?
cards.answer: Evaluating employees against goals they set jointly with their manager.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.10 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.10 Performance Rating Methods: Forced Choice, Checklist, Standards, and Objectives
points: Employee input prevents unfair standards and builds commitment
distractors: Evaluating employees by fitting all of their ratings to a set curve.
Rating how often each desired behavior occurs on the job over time.
Comparing each employee with every other employee in the unit in pairs.

cards.front: What is the work standards method best suited for?
cards.answer: Production jobs where output can be precisely measured against targets.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.10 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.10 Performance Rating Methods: Forced Choice, Checklist, Standards, and Objectives
points: Example: 30 parts/hour minimal, 40 good, 50 outstanding
distractors: Knowledge jobs where creativity and judgment drive the results.
Management jobs where leadership behaviors matter most of all.
Team jobs where results can't be traced to any one individual.

cards.front: What is forced distribution, and its main drawback?
cards.answer: Fitting ratings to a set curve (e.g., 20/70/10); it erodes teamwork and demotivates good performers.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.11 Performance Ranking Methods
points: Chemtura dropped it
Termination quotas invite legal risk
distractors: Rating each person against fixed standards; its main drawback is that it takes too long to complete.
Letting employees set goals with managers; its main drawback is that goals are often too easy.
Rating how often desired behaviors occur; its main drawback is that it costs too much to develop.

cards.front: What are forced ranking and paired comparison?
cards.answer: Forced ranking orders people best to worst; paired comparison compares each person with every other.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.11 Performance Ranking Methods
points: Both are ranking methods; impractical for large groups
distractors: Forced ranking compares each person with every other; paired comparison orders people best to worst.
Forced ranking fits ratings to a curve; paired comparison anchors each point with a behavior example.
Forced ranking uses goals set with the manager; paired comparison uses peers' ratings of teamwork.

cards.front: What does Wells Fargo show about performance goals and ethics?
cards.answer: Aggressive cross-sell goals tied to pay overwhelmed ethics training and led to fake accounts.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.12 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.12 Predicting Deviance
points: Performance management shouldn't just extract more from people
distractors: Its ethics training was so strong that aggressive cross-sell goals had no effect on behavior.
Low, easy goals bored employees, so they opened fake accounts to keep themselves busy.
Fake accounts came from outside fraud, not goals; employees were cleared of any wrongdoing.

cards.front: What's the problem with using one rating for both pay and development?
cards.answer: Managers must choose between honest-but-low feedback and a raise, so ratings get inflated.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.13 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.13 Improving Performance Through Feedback and Rewards
points: United Airlines decoupled ratings from pay
distractors: One rating makes reviews too short, since managers skip development when pay isn't involved.
Using one rating is illegal under the Equal Pay Act, since pay must be set separately by HR.
One rating causes deflation, since managers give low scores to save money on annual raises.

cards.front: What are the three steps of the performance review process?
cards.answer: Preparation, communication (the meeting), and follow-through.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.14 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.14 Performance Review Process
points: Prep: gather all sources incl. self-evaluation
Follow-through: regular coaching and praise
distractors: Rating, ranking, and then rewarding each employee.
Goal setting, coaching, and then the discipline steps.
Self-review, peer review, and then supervisor review.

cards.front: What makes feedback effective?
cards.answer: Focus on behavior, compare to goals not people, be specific about desired behavior, and limit the points.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.14 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.14 Performance Review Process
points: Jointly set goals; be supportive
At most three improvement areas
distractors: Focus on personality, compare to coworkers, keep it general, and cover every issue at once.
Start with criticism, compare to the top performer, avoid specifics, and save it for yearly reviews.
Focus on attitude, compare to past reviews, be vague about fixes, and include pay changes each time.

cards.front: What is constructive feedback?
cards.answer: Feedback that addresses behavior with examples of how to correct it, never attacking the person.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.14 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.14 Performance Review Process
points: Give both positive and negative feedback
distractors: Feedback that names the person's character flaws so they understand why they keep failing.
Feedback that offers only praise so the employee stays positive and motivated at work.
Feedback given in public so other employees can learn from one person's mistakes.

cards.front: When is negative feedback most likely to be accepted?
cards.answer: When it's objective, from a credible source, tactful, and impersonal.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.14 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.14 Performance Review Process
points: Let employees explain their performance first
distractors: When it's subjective, comes from a peer, and is blunt and personal.
When it's delivered in public in front of the whole team at once.
When it's general, comes as a surprise, and is tied to a pay cut.

cards.front: Why should managers start a review by asking employees to describe their performance?
cards.answer: Letting employees explain raises satisfaction with the review and attitudes toward the manager.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.14 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.14 Performance Review Process
points: Ask about obstacles too
distractors: Employees describing their own performance lowers their satisfaction but makes the review faster to finish.
It's legally required, since employees must speak first under federal performance review rules.
Self-descriptions replace the manager's rating, so the manager doesn't need to prepare beforehand.

cards.front: Why do nonmonetary rewards matter in performance management?
cards.answer: Specific praise and appreciation are motivating; lack of recognition is a top employee complaint.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.14 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.14 Performance Review Process
points: Recognize improvement as well as achievement
distractors: They matter only for low-wage jobs, since higher earners care only about money and bonuses.
They're required by law, since the FLSA mandates written recognition for nonexempt employees.
They don't matter much, since recognition rarely affects motivation once pay is competitive.

cards.front: How can the same feedback be read differently across cultures?
cards.answer: 'Room for improvement, but overall good' reads as criticism to many Chinese and Korean managers.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.14 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.14 Performance Review Process
points: Many U.S. managers read it literally as praise
Match wording to the listener's interpretive style
distractors: 'Room for improvement, but overall good' reads as high praise to many Chinese and Korean managers.
Feedback is read the same way across all cultures, since direct criticism is universally understood.
'Needs improvement' reads as a promotion signal to many German and Dutch managers in reviews.

cards.front: What is continuous performance management?
cards.answer: Year-round check-ins, coaching, and feedback, with employees helping set goals, replacing the annual review.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.15 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.15 Continuous Performance Management
points: Adobe: voluntary turnover −30%
Not for everyone: Intel reinstated scores
distractors: An annual review done four times a year, with managers alone setting all goals and final ratings.
A system that ranks employees continuously, cutting the bottom 10% each quarter instead of yearly.
A year-round self-review program that replaces managers' feedback with peer ratings and surveys.

cards.front: What is the primary goal of an appraisal discussion?
cards.answer: Enabling improvement so the employee and organization succeed; second is a legally defensible record.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.16 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.16 Improvement and Development Plans
points: Not about punishment
distractors: Setting next year's pay raise; the second goal is ranking the employee against their coworkers.
Creating a legally defensible record; enabling improvement is secondary to protecting the firm.
Deciding whether to promote or terminate, since the review exists mainly to sort employees.

cards.front: What is the difference between a performance problem and a behavior problem?
cards.answer: Performance: can't demonstrate mastery of tasks. Behavior: does the tasks but disrupts the workplace.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.16 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.16 Improvement and Development Plans
points: Classify the problem before corrective action
distractors: Performance: does tasks but disrupts the workplace. Behavior: can't demonstrate mastery of tasks.
Performance: poor attendance and lateness. Behavior: poor quality of work and missed deadlines.
Performance problems are handled by HR; behavior problems are handled only by the employee's peers.

cards.front: What is a performance improvement plan (PIP)?
cards.answer: A tool to monitor and measure deficient work and set how it will be corrected, by when, and with what support.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.16 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.16 Improvement and Development Plans
points: Fields: needs, objectives/metrics, actions, timeframe, signatures
Build it with the employee for commitment
distractors: A plan to make good performance even better by building new skills for a future promotion or new role.
A document that ends employment immediately, stating the reasons and the date of the final paycheck.
A training course for underperformers that replaces any need for documentation or later follow-up.

cards.front: What does FOSA+ stand for?
cards.answer: Facts, objectives, solutions, actions (consequences), plus your overall support.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.16 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.16 Improvement and Development Plans
points: Structures corrective and rule-violation meetings
distractors: Feedback, objectives, standards, and assessment, plus your overall summary.
Facts, opinions, sanctions, alternatives, plus your overall summary rating.
Focus, observe, support, and act, plus your overall plan for development.

cards.front: What is an employee development plan?
cards.answer: A plan to make good performance even better, rather than fix a deficiency.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.16 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.16 Improvement and Development Plans
points: InterContinental Hotels Group personal development plans
distractors: A plan to fix deficient work and set how and when it will be corrected.
A plan listing increasingly severe steps for repeated workplace problems.
A plan for replacing key leaders quickly when their positions open up.

cards.front: What is progressive discipline?
cards.answer: Increasingly severe measures when an employee fails to correct a problem after a reasonable chance.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline
points: Uses the least severe action needed
Requires a legitimate reason (just cause)
distractors: Firing an employee immediately for any violation to set an example for other employees.
A plan to make good performance even better through development and new assignments.
Applying the same penalty to every offense regardless of how many times it has happened.

cards.front: What is the purpose of progressive discipline?
cards.answer: To alert the employee to a problem, start with the least severe step, and escalate only if it isn't fixed.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline
points: Correction, not punishment
Also creates fairness and legal documentation
distractors: To punish the employee quickly with the most severe step, so the problem isn't repeated by others.
To build a record for termination, so the employee is let go as soon as possible after a problem.
To replace coaching with formal steps, so managers don't have to discuss problems informally.

cards.front: Why not just fire an underperformer on the spot?
cards.answer: Progressive discipline gives a fair chance to improve first and documents just cause if firing is needed.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline; 8.21 Legal and Ethical Issues in Performance Management
points: Serious offenses can still skip steps
distractors: Firing on the spot is illegal in every state, since at-will employment requires a written warning first.
Progressive discipline saves money, since suspended employees are paid less than terminated ones.
On-the-spot firing is fine for any issue, since documentation isn't needed for at-will employees.

cards.front: What are the four typical steps of progressive discipline?
cards.answer: Counseling, written warning, suspension without pay, and termination.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline
points: Escalate only if the problem continues
distractors: Written warning, counseling, termination, and suspension with pay.
Verbal warning, demotion, transfer, and termination with severance.
Counseling, suspension without pay, written warning, and termination.

cards.front: What is the counseling step of progressive discipline?
cards.answer: An informal talk that raises the problem before it needs a written warning; it needn't be documented.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline
points: The least severe step
distractors: A formal written warning placed in the employee's file, with consequences and a firm timeframe.
A one- to three-day unpaid suspension that shows the employee the problem is serious now.
A final meeting where the employee is told they're terminated, with written notice afterward.

cards.front: What does a written warning contain?
cards.answer: The problem's history, the employee's explanation, expectations, consequences, and a timeframe; it's filed.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline
points: May be repeated with stronger wording (final warning)
distractors: Only the date and the manager's signature, since details could be used against the company in court.
A verbal reminder of the rule with no explanation from the employee, kept in the manager's notes.
The employee's full performance history, pay record, and medical file, sent to every coworker.

cards.front: How long is a typical disciplinary suspension?
cards.answer: Usually less than a week, often one to three days without pay; the act matters more than the length.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline
points: A written record is given at the start and filed
distractors: Usually two to four weeks without pay; a longer suspension sends a much clearer message to others.
Usually one to three days with full pay, so the employee isn't punished financially for the problem.
Usually a full month without pay; anything shorter has little effect on the employee's behavior.

cards.front: What should happen before termination in progressive discipline?
cards.answer: The employee gets a chance to explain and a fair investigation, then written notice afterward.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline
points: Used when earlier steps fail
distractors: Nothing; the manager should end employment immediately and skip any investigation to avoid delays.
The employee's coworkers vote on whether termination is fair, then HR sends written notice.
A paid suspension of at least a month, then termination by phone with no written notice.

cards.front: Which progressive discipline steps can be repeated?
cards.answer: The text says the written warning can repeat; the quiz's likely answer is written warning and suspension.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline
points: Moderate confidence on the quiz pairing
The second written warning is the 'final warning'
distractors: None; each step can be used only once, so a second problem always moves to the next step.
Counseling and termination can repeat; written warnings and suspensions can be used once only.
The text says only termination can repeat; the quiz likely answer is counseling and suspension.

cards.front: When can progressive discipline skip steps?
cards.answer: For serious offenses like fighting, harassment, or drug use; minor issues start at the lowest step.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline
points: Some firms suspend with pay first; the process isn't rigid
distractors: Never; every offense must start at counseling, even for violence, harassment, or drug use.
For any second offense, even minor ones like lateness, since repeating means skipping ahead.
Only when the employee is on probation; long-tenured staff must always go step by step.

cards.front: What should a manager do in every disciplinary meeting?
cards.answer: State the behavior with examples, explain the standard, let the employee explain, and set expectations calmly.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline
points: Include timeframe and consequences
Have a witness or note taker
distractors: State the employee's personality flaws, compare them to coworkers, and announce the penalty without discussion.
Keep the problem vague to avoid conflict, skip the employee's side, and end with a reminder of pay.
Let HR lead the meeting alone, avoid giving examples, and set expectations only in a later email.

cards.front: What is Frito-Lay's 'Discipline Without Punishment'?
cards.answer: Oral reminder, written reminder, then a paid one-day suspension to write a commitment to change.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline
points: No letter = resignation accepted
distractors: Verbal warning, written warning, then an unpaid one-week suspension and a final warning.
Counseling, demotion, then a transfer to another unit with a commitment to change.
Written reminder, final warning, then termination with severance pay and references.

cards.front: How can performance management improve collaboration, as at Prudential?
cards.answer: Make collaborative behavior part of assessments, give feedback on it, and hold supervisors accountable.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.18 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.18 Case Study: Improving Collaboration Through Performance Management
points: Prudential addresses toxic behavior with improvement plans the employee chooses
distractors: Use forced ranking among teammates, so collaborators compete to show who contributes most.
Remove collaboration from reviews, since it can't be measured objectively in a fair way.
Reward only individual results, so stars help others voluntarily without formal goals.

cards.front: What are the three common obstacles to effective performance management?
cards.answer: Not communicating a performance plan, lack of accountability, and human biases and errors.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.19 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.19 Performance Management Obstacles
points: 'Human capacity limitations' is not one of them
distractors: Too much feedback, too many rating sources, and overly specific goals for every employee.
Lack of software, high cost of reviews, and employees who refuse to set their own goals.
Too much accountability, too many coaching sessions, and lack of a forced ranking system.

cards.front: What is a performance plan?
cards.answer: A plan of goals, how results are measured and weighted, and standards for the period, made with the employee.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.19 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.19 Performance Management Obstacles
points: Usually a year, but matches the period (6-month project, 6-month plan)
distractors: A plan to correct deficient work, with consequences, deadlines, and the support offered for improvement.
A plan listing which employees will be promoted and when, based on their potential and readiness.
A training calendar listing every course an employee must complete during the coming review year.

cards.front: What is accountability in performance management?
cards.answer: Regularly answering to a superior for results and being held responsible for them.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.19 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.19 Performance Management Obstacles
points: Hold managers accountable for regular, accurate feedback
Locate ownership of the system at a senior level
distractors: Setting goals jointly with a manager and tracking progress on them throughout the year.
Being free to choose your own goals without having to report results to anyone above you.
Answering to peers for teamwork behaviors, rated through anonymous 360-degree feedback.

cards.front: How do performance reviews differ from coaching?
cards.answer: Reviews look back periodically; coaching is more frequent, forward-looking, and reinforces behavior.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.19 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.19 Performance Management Obstacles
points: Online tools help but can't replace face-to-face talks
distractors: Coaching looks back periodically; reviews are more frequent, forward-looking, and reinforce behavior.
Reviews are done by peers; coaching is done by HR, so the two never involve the same people.
Reviews focus on development only; coaching focuses only on pay and promotion decisions.

cards.front: How can organizations minimize rating biases?
cards.answer: Rater training, year-round documentation, clear goals, and standards based on observable behavior.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.20 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.20 Human Biases and Errors
points: Train raters on what each rating level means
distractors: Forced distribution, year-end memory, vague goals, and standards based on personality traits.
Having the same rater for everyone, removing documentation, and using only self-ratings.
Rating only once a year, using personality standards, and skipping any training for raters.

cards.front: What is the contrast effect?
cards.answer: Rating someone by comparison with other employees instead of against standards.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.20 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.20 Human Biases and Errors
points: 'Rosa beats the others'
distractors: Letting the most recent events weigh too heavily in an overall rating.
Letting one positive trait inflate the ratings on every other dimension.
Rating everyone in the middle of the scale to avoid giving extreme scores.

cards.front: What is the recency effect, and how do you prevent it?
cards.answer: Recent events weigh too heavily; prevent it by recording performance regularly.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.20 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.20 Human Biases and Errors
points: First impression bias is the opposite: early events dominate
distractors: Early judgments color later ratings; prevent it by delaying the first review for six months.
One trait inflates every rating; prevent it by rating each dimension on a separate day.
Comparing to coworkers; prevent it by rating each employee against written standards.

cards.front: What is the halo effect?
cards.answer: One positive characteristic inflates the ratings on everything else.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.20 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.20 Human Biases and Errors
points: Likable Leon isn't necessarily productive
distractors: One negative characteristic lowers the ratings on all else.
Recent events weigh too heavily in the overall rating given.
Early judgments about someone color all later assessments.

cards.front: What is the horns effect?
cards.answer: One negative characteristic lowers the ratings on everything else.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.20 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.20 Human Biases and Errors
points: Often-late Pat isn't necessarily unproductive
distractors: One positive characteristic inflates ratings on everything.
Rating everyone too high to avoid conflict during reviews.
Early judgments about someone color all of the later ratings.

cards.front: What is the high potential error?
cards.answer: Rating someone on their promise or potential rather than their actual performance.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.20 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.20 Human Biases and Errors
points: Confusing training scores with realized results
distractors: Giving higher ratings to people who resemble the rater in background or hobbies.
Rating someone by comparison with other employees instead of against standards.
Ignoring factors beyond the employee's control, like a broken machine, in ratings.

cards.front: What are leniency error and central tendency?
cards.answer: Leniency: rating everyone too high. Central tendency: rating everyone in the middle.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.20 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.20 Human Biases and Errors
points: Leniency avoids conflict
Central tendency: belief no one deserves the top
distractors: Leniency: rating everyone in the middle. Central tendency: rating everyone too high.
Leniency: rating by potential. Central tendency: rating by comparison with coworkers.
Leniency: rating strictly low. Central tendency: rating everyone by their most recent work.

cards.front: What is the similar-to-me effect?
cards.answer: Giving higher ratings to people who resemble the rater, such as the same school or hobbies.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.20 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.20 Human Biases and Errors
points: Also a diversity and legal risk
distractors: Rating someone by comparison with other employees instead of against written standards.
Early judgments about an employee that color all later assessments throughout the year.
Assuming an individual has traits associated with their group, like gender or age group.

cards.front: What is opportunity bias?
cards.answer: Ignoring factors beyond the employee's control, like a broken machine, when rating.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.20 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.20 Human Biases and Errors
points: Don't penalize what employees can't control
distractors: Rating someone on their promise or potential rather than actual performance.
Giving higher ratings to people who resemble the rater in background or hobbies.
Rating someone by comparing them to coworkers instead of to written standards.

cards.front: What is stereotyping in performance ratings?
cards.answer: Assuming an individual has traits associated with their group, such as rating male servers lower on service.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.20 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.20 Human Biases and Errors
points: Also a legal risk
distractors: Giving higher ratings to people who resemble the rater, such as those who attended the same school or college.
Ignoring factors beyond the employee's control, like a broken machine or missing supplies, when rating them.
Rating someone by comparison with other employees on the team instead of against the written standards.

cards.front: What is first impression bias?
cards.answer: Early judgments about an employee color all later assessments.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.20 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.20 Human Biases and Errors
points: A slow starter who became strong gets underrated
distractors: Recent events outweigh the rest of the year's work.
One trait inflates the ratings on every other dimension.
Rating everyone in the middle to avoid any conflict at all.

cards.front: Which law covers age discrimination claims arising from appraisals?
cards.answer: The Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA), not Title VII as the book says.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.21 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 8.21 Legal and Ethical Issues in Performance Management
points: Erratum: book says an age claim 'may be supported by Title VII'
Disproportionately low ratings for a protected group draw scrutiny
distractors: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as the book says, since it covers age claims.
The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), which covers age-related conditions at work.
The Equal Pay Act, since age claims from appraisals involve pay differences by age group.

cards.front: What is retaliation in performance appraisal?
cards.answer: Giving low ratings to punish someone who opposed discrimination or filed with the EEOC; it's illegal.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.21 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 8.21 Legal and Ethical Issues in Performance Management
points: Applies to Title VII and age-discrimination complaints
distractors: Giving low ratings to an employee who performed poorly after training; it's legal if documented.
Rating someone lower because of their age or disability; it's disparate treatment, not retaliation.
Giving high ratings to avoid an EEOC complaint; it's illegal because it inflates the employee's record.

cards.front: What is negligent performance appraisal?
cards.answer: A claim for skipping or botching required evaluations when severe emotional distress was foreseeable.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.21 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 8.21 Legal and Ethical Issues in Performance Management
points: Must prove duty of care, breach, foreseeable injury, causation
distractors: A claim for rating someone lower because of their race or sex under federal anti-discrimination law.
A claim for giving low ratings to punish an employee who filed a charge with the EEOC earlier.
A claim that ratings were too high, which later made it difficult for the company to fire the employee.

cards.front: What makes a performance appraisal system legally defensible?
cards.answer: Job-analysis criteria, trained raters with firsthand knowledge, chances to improve, and documented specifics.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.21 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 8.21 Legal and Ethical Issues in Performance Management
points: Objective criteria; no disparate impact
'Never any surprises at a performance review'
distractors: Personality-based criteria, ratings by HR only, no chance to improve, and general overall impressions.
Forced distribution, secret ratings, a single annual meeting, and ratings based on potential alone.
Self-ratings only, raters without contact with the employee, and documentation added after a lawsuit.

cards.front: How did Microsoft redesign performance management?
cards.answer: It dropped forced 1-5 ratings for Talent Talks on impact, helping others, and using others' work, plus check-ins.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.22 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.22 Real World Response: Improving Culture through Performance Management at Microsoft
points: 'Perspectives' tool for requested peer feedback
distractors: It added a forced 1-5 stack ranking with annual reviews, tying every rating directly to bonus pools.
It moved to self-ratings only, dropping manager feedback and check-ins to reduce time spent on reviews.
It kept stack ranking but made it quarterly, so low performers were identified and cut more quickly.

cards.front: What are feedback seeking, avoiding, and mitigating?
cards.answer: Seeking: asking after success. Avoiding: dodging after failure. Mitigating: excuses to manage impressions.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.23 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.23 Strategic HRM Exercise: Your Feedback Seeking Behavior
points: Avoiding feedback deprives you of improvement information
distractors: Seeking: excuses after failure. Avoiding: asking after success. Mitigating: dodging all feedback.
Seeking: asking after failure. Avoiding: dodging after success. Mitigating: praise from peers.
Seeking: waiting for annual reviews. Avoiding: skipping reviews. Mitigating: appealing a rating.

cards.front: What should you do if your job has no goals or feedback?
cards.answer: Create your own: pick your top three outcomes, set measurable goals, and track them objectively.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.23 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.23 Strategic HRM Exercise: Your Feedback Seeking Behavior
points: Example: survey questions to track staff engagement
distractors: Wait for the annual review, since setting your own goals can conflict with your manager's plans.
Ask coworkers to rate you, since peer opinions replace the need for any measurable goals.
Focus on staying busy, since visible effort is the best measure when no goals are set.

cards.front: Jordan is always busy, stays late, and answers every email within minutes, but his projects rarely move company goals. What does this illustrate?
choices: Long hours prove his high performance level
Busy employees always contribute to goals
cards.explanation: Performance management separates activity from results: being busy doesn't mean contributing to organizational goals.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.4 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.4 Why Is Performance Management Important?

cards.front: Which statement about performance management is TRUE?
choices: Its data can be used to benchmark best practices
It's essentially the same as measuring behaviors
Being busy means an employee is contributing
It focuses only on individual employees
cards.explanation: Generating useful data, like benchmarks, is one of its three benefits. It also covers teams, units, and processes, and it measures results, not just behaviors.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.4 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.4 Why Is Performance Management Important?

cards.front: Which statement about performance management is FALSE?
choices: Its main aim is all parts working toward results
Its data can show whether training paid off
It's essentially the same as measuring behaviors
Clear goals and feedback are powerful motivators
cards.explanation: It's false that performance management is just measuring behaviors; behaviors aren't results. The other three are true.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.4 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.4 Why Is Performance Management Important?

cards.front: A COO wants every department's goals to roll up to the company's three strategic priorities. Which benefit of performance management is she after?
choices: Aligning organizational, team, and individual goals
Generating benchmarking data for outside reports
cards.explanation: Aligning goals across levels with the strategy is the first of the three benefits.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.4 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.4 Why Is Performance Management Important?

cards.front: After a new safety program, a plant uses performance data to compare accident rates before and after. Which benefit is this?
choices: Useful data to judge change efforts
cards.explanation: Useful data lets firms benchmark, judge change efforts like training or safety programs, and compute ROI.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.4 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.4 Why Is Performance Management Important?

cards.front: A software team's members each hit personal targets, but the release keeps slipping because no one helps anyone else. What's the fix?
choices: Rank team members against each other
Remove all goals from the team
cards.explanation: For interdependent work, give team-level as well as individual goals and feedback; individual stars can hurt the team.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.4 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.4 Why Is Performance Management Important?

cards.front: A bank tracks staff skills, loan-processing time, client retention, and return on capital as one linked system. What tool is this?
cards.explanation: Those are the learning/growth, internal process, customer, and financial perspectives of Kaplan and Norton's balanced scorecard.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.5 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.5 Balanced Scorecard

cards.front: Priya and her manager set a goal: "Cut average ticket resolution time by 20% this quarter." She believes it's important and doable. Per research, how does it help her?
choices: It replaces the need for any formal performance appraisal
It guarantees a raise once the quarter is over
It focuses her and sustains effort through setbacks
It makes everyone on the team work in one identical style
cards.explanation: Specific, challenging goals focus attention, increase effort, sustain persistence through setbacks, and prompt new strategies.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.7 Apply · Motivational Concepts
cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards

cards.front: Which goal is the most SMART?
choices: Do a better job with customers this year
Try hard to improve sales whenever possible
Be the best salesperson in the company
cards.explanation: Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound: a clear metric and a deadline.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.7 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards

cards.front: A manager wants a goal that is clear and easy to understand. Which SMART element is that?
cards.explanation: Specific means clear, understandable, and stretching.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.7 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards

cards.front: A director hands down a stretch goal nobody believes is possible, and effort collapses. What was missing?
choices: A larger number of goals to spread effort
Vaguer wording so no one can fail at it
cards.explanation: Commitment matters most for difficult goals, and it's highest when people believe the goal is important and attainable.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.7 Apply · Motivational Concepts
cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards

cards.front: A lender pays loan officers only for loan volume, and approval standards quietly slip. What does this show?
choices: Goals have no real effect on behavior
cards.explanation: Goal-linked incentives strongly shape behavior; narrow or overly ambitious goals can push risky or unethical acts (as in the 2008 mortgage crisis).
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.7 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards

cards.front: A unit head lists 11 top priorities for the year. What would Ritz-Carlton's approach suggest?
choices: Cut to three to focus resources
Add more so that nothing gets missed
Keep all 11 but weight them equally
Drop goals and rely on feedback
cards.explanation: Ritz-Carlton allows at most three priorities per unit: beyond three you diffuse resources.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.7 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.7 Setting Goals and Standards

cards.front: A manager and an analyst jointly agree on four quarterly goals, and the analyst picks how to reach them. Which method is this?
cards.explanation: MBO evaluates against mutually set goals; employee input and choice of methods build commitment.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.10 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.10 Performance Rating Methods: Forced Choice, Checklist, Standards, and Objectives

cards.front: Noor designs product packaging alongside two engineers daily, and a retail buyer approves her final designs. Who is an appropriate source of performance information?
choices: A new hire from another division
An engineer who works with her daily
The payroll clerk who processes her pay
A VP who has never seen her work
cards.explanation: Choose raters with task acquaintance: people who actually observe the work.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources

cards.front: Which rater would be the WEAKEST source of performance information about a nurse?
choices: A patient asked about her courtesy
An executive who has never seen her work
The charge nurse who supervises her shifts
A fellow nurse on the same unit
cards.explanation: Without task acquaintance, a rater can't judge accurately. Supervisors, peers, and customers (on interpersonal behavior) can.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources

cards.front: A company wants feedback on how its managers lead, communicate, and treat their teams. Which source fits best, and what's critical?
choices: The CEO, using last year's data
cards.explanation: Upward reviews by subordinates assess leadership; anonymity is critical because people fear retaliation.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources

cards.front: A hotel asks guests to rate front-desk staff. What should the survey ask guests about?
cards.explanation: External customers are best asked about interpersonal behavior; they can't separate the employee from rules and resources.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources

cards.front: On a tightly interdependent product team, who usually knows the most about a member's day-to-day contribution?
cards.explanation: Peers see task and interpersonal behavior the boss may miss and are most knowledgeable in interdependent work.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources

cards.front: Mateo rates himself 5 out of 5 on everything, while his peers and supervisor rate him around 3. What does this illustrate?
choices: That supervisors shouldn't rate their staff
Proof that peer ratings are always biased
cards.explanation: Self-assessment adds information and opens dialogue, but people often rate themselves too high or too low.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources

cards.front: Which principle should guide which sources contribute to someone's appraisal?
choices: Convenience: whoever is free that week
Task acquaintance: how much they see of the work
Popularity: whoever knows the person socially
cards.explanation: Choose and weight sources by credibility and their opportunity to observe the work (task acquaintance).
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.8 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.8 Performance Information Sources

cards.front: Kenji's goal is to raise webinar sign-ups 15%. Which manager comment is the most effective feedback?
choices: Your landing pages need to be better
Move the sign-up button above the fold
Great work lately, just keep doing what you're doing
You're such a team player, everyone likes you
cards.explanation: Effective feedback is specific, actionable, and tied to the goal. The others are vague, about the person, or lack the how.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.14 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.14 Performance Review Process

cards.front: Which of these is INEFFECTIVE feedback?
choices: "Send drafts by Thursday so I can review them."
"Add a one-line summary at the top of each report."
"Cite the data source under each chart."
cards.explanation: 'Need to be better' is vague and gives no actionable direction; the others are specific about the desired behavior.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.14 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.14 Performance Review Process

cards.front: A manager tells an employee, "You're lazy and careless." What's the main problem?
choices: It compares to goals instead of to peers
It focuses on too few improvement areas
It attacks character instead of behavior
It's too specific about the behavior
cards.explanation: Feedback should be constructive: address behavior with correction examples, never attack the person.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.14 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.14 Performance Review Process

cards.front: A supervisor sets clear quarterly goals but never checks in until the year-end review. What's the likely result?
choices: Higher morale, since check-ins feel like micromanaging
No effect, since feedback matters only for pay
Peak results, since goals alone drive performance
cards.explanation: Goals direct effort, but feedback tracks progress toward them so people can adjust. Goals without feedback don't work well.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.14 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.14 Performance Review Process

cards.front: In a review, a manager lists nine things the employee should fix. What does the text advise instead?
choices: Focus on at most three areas
Add more items so nothing is missed
Skip negatives and give praise only
Compare the employee to top peers
cards.explanation: Limit feedback to a few focused points (at most three) to avoid overwhelm and defensiveness.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.14 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.14 Performance Review Process

cards.front: Which comparison makes feedback most effective?
choices: Performance vs. goals and past performance
Performance vs. the team's top performer
Performance vs. the manager's own early career
Performance vs. a coworker in another unit
cards.explanation: Frame feedback against goals, past performance, and improvement rate, and minimize comparisons to other people.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.14 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.14 Performance Review Process

cards.front: A manager writes a U.S.-style review for a Korean employee: "There's room for improvement, but overall this is good." What's the risk?
choices: She may read it as feedback on poor work
She'll read it as the highest possible praise
cards.explanation: Many Chinese and Korean managers read this phrasing as signaling relatively poor performance; match wording to the listener.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.14 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.14 Performance Review Process

cards.front: A firm swaps its annual review for monthly check-ins, coaching, and employee-set goals. What is this?
cards.explanation: Ongoing, year-round coaching and feedback with employee input is continuous performance management.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.15 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.15 Continuous Performance Management

cards.front: A friend scoffs, "Why not just fire underperformers on the spot?" Which best explains progressive discipline's purpose?
choices: It alerts them first and escalates only if needed
It punishes people so they feel the cost of mistakes
It ensures every employee is eventually suspended
It replaces the need for any documentation
cards.explanation: Progressive discipline alerts the employee, starts with the least severe step, and escalates only without improvement.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline

cards.front: Which statement does NOT describe the purpose of progressive discipline?
choices: It starts with the least severe action possible
It escalates only if earlier steps don't work
It's mainly a tool to punish employees for mistakes
It alerts employees to a problem needing correction
cards.explanation: Progressive discipline is about correction, not punishment.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline

cards.front: An employee is late twice in a month. Where should progressive discipline start, and why?
choices: Termination: to set an example for others
Written warning: to skip the informal talk
Suspension: to show the rule is serious
cards.explanation: Minor issues start at the lowest step; use the least severe action needed to stimulate improvement.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline

cards.front: Before disciplining Lee, his manager checks whether he lacks the skill or is disrupting the team despite having it. Why?
choices: To skip the improvement plan entirely
To set his forced-distribution rank for the year
To classify the type of problem
To decide which coworker should be blamed
cards.explanation: Corrective action starts by classifying a performance problem (can't do) vs. a behavior problem (can, but disrupts).
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.16 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.16 Improvement and Development Plans

cards.front: A manager meets Ana with the facts of the problem, the objectives, solutions, consequences if it isn't fixed, and her support. Which framework is this?
cards.explanation: FOSA+ = Facts, Objectives, Solutions, Actions (consequences), plus support.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.16 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.16 Improvement and Development Plans

cards.front: After repeated performance problems, Dev is sent home for two days without pay. Which step is this?
cards.explanation: Time off without pay, usually one to three days, is the suspension step.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline

cards.front: Rina's manager has an informal chat to bring a missed-deadline pattern to her attention. Which step is this?
cards.explanation: Raising the problem informally before any written warning is counseling.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline

cards.front: Omar receives a formal document listing the problem's history, his explanation, the required changes, consequences, and a deadline. Which step is this?
cards.explanation: A filed document with history, explanation, expectations, consequences, and a timeframe is a written warning.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline

cards.front: After counseling, two written warnings, and a suspension, Jess still hasn't improved and is let go after a chance to explain. Which step is this?
cards.explanation: Termination follows when earlier steps fail, after a fair investigation and a chance to explain.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline

cards.front: Which sequence shows the typical progressive discipline process?
cards.explanation: The typical order runs from least to most severe.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline

cards.front: An employee punches a coworker on the warehouse floor. Must the manager start with counseling?
choices: No; fighting can only lead to counseling
No; serious offenses can skip steps
Yes; every step must always be used in order
Yes; but only after two written warnings
cards.explanation: Progressive discipline isn't rigid. Serious offenses (fighting, harassment, drug use) may skip steps.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline

cards.front: A manager issues a written warning that says, "This is a final warning; another violation will result in suspension." What does this show?
choices: Counseling has been skipped, which is illegal
cards.explanation: The text says the written warning step can repeat; the second becomes a final warning.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.17 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.17 Progressive Discipline

cards.front: Which situation is an obstacle to effective performance management?
choices: Consistent goals and criteria across teams
Employees never told how they'll be measured
cards.explanation: Not communicating a performance plan (goals, measures, standards) is one of the three common obstacles.
cards.subtitle: Ch 8.19 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 8.19 Performance Management Obstacles

cards.front: A supervisor never addresses poor performance because she wants to keep the team atmosphere positive. Which obstacle is this?
cards.explanation: Managers who aren't held responsible for regular, accurate feedback avoid tough conversations: a lack of accountability.

cards.note: Read more: 8.19 Performance Management Obstacles

cards.front: Leon is charming and well liked, so his manager rates him high on productivity, which is actually average. Which error is this?

No way to tell any employees apart
